The dead tones have pitch shapes 55, 33, 31. Dead tones occur with either lax or tense vowel syllables. Tones are instable in Bugan, a part of the lexicon can be pronounced with either of two tones ... (p. 141) ... 2.1.2.2. Derived words. new_statements.rule_in_words: Bugan is described as a lexical-tone language (five full tones on open syllables, three on checked syllables). The source makes no statement about word stress or accent; the only prominence-related fact is that a toneless 'slight tone' (i.e. a neutral/atonic, reduced syllable) is restricted to a subset of prefixal first syllables (pə⁰-, tə⁰-, lə⁰-, tse⁰-), while roots/main syllables always bear a full tone — consistent with the Austroasiatic weak-presyllable + full main-syllable word shape, but not stated as a stress rule by the author.
new_statements.exceptions: Most prefixes carry a full lexical tone (pə⁵⁵-, te⁵⁵-, na³³-, mu³³-, pu⁵⁵- etc.); only 'a few' take the slight (neutral) tone. Tones are unstable (many words have two alternative tones) and undergo progressive sandhi in context.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms (monosyllables and prefix+root disyllables) from the Nala-area variety, 1994 fieldwork; tone values in context differ from citation values (sandhi).
new_statements.identity_note: Li 1996 (and Li & Luo 2015) describe the Nala-area variety of Guangnan County (autonym pə⁵⁵kan³³; six tones incl. neutral). Li Yunbing 2005 describes the Manlong 曼龙 variety of Xichou County (autonym pu⁵⁵qeŋ⁴⁴; four tones 55/44/24/31). Both fall under glottocode buga1247 (no dialect-level codes in Glottolog); Li 1996 claims 'There is no variation in the Bugan language', Hsiu 2016 reports speakers acknowledge some internal variation.

sources.note: Nothing explicit about stress or accent (full scanned a full-text search for stress/accent: no 'stress'/'accent'). Sec. 1.3 Tones (p. 141): six 'live' tones 55, 33, 35, 13, 31 plus 'the slight tone (atonality) ø' which 'appears only in some prefixes'; dead (checked) tones 55/33/31; tones unstable and subject to sandhi. Sec. 2.1.2.2 (p. 144): 'All prefixes are pronounced with tone, but a few of them are pronounced with the slight tone.' Nala variety (Guangnan), 1994 fieldwork.
